```{r setup, include=FALSE}
library(here)
library(tidyverse)
library(patchwork)
library(dagitty)
source(here("code", "dag-helpers.R"))

knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  echo = FALSE,
  warning = FALSE,
  message = FALSE,
  fig.align = "center",
  out.width = "100%"
)

theme_blue <- "#377eb8"
theme_red  <- "#ED1B2F"
job_cols   <- c(Reviewer = theme_blue, Panelist = theme_red)

# simulated (NOT real CIHR) data -- see code/ror-sim-deviate.R
d <- read_csv(here("data", "sim-deviate.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  mutate(
    job = factor(job, levels = c("reviewer", "panelist"),
      labels = c("Reviewer", "Panelist")),
    exp = factor(exp, levels = c("high", "med", "low", "none"),
      labels = c("High", "Medium", "Low", "Not enough"))
  )
```

## The problem {.vcenter}

::::::: roomy
:::::: msg-list
::: msg-item
**Scores decide who gets funded**\
Peer review moves billions of research dollars
:::

::: msg-item
**Scores come out of a conversation**\
Panel discussion can change what reviewers think
:::

::: msg-item
**Not everyone in that conversation is equally engaged**\
Some members read the application closely; most did not
:::
::::::
:::::::

::: notes
(~1:00) Open with the stakes. Funding decisions rest on scores, but those scores
are not just averages of independent opinions -- they are shaped by a group
discussion. And the people in the room differ in how much they actually know about
the application in front of them. That difference is our question.
:::

## How CIHR Project Grant review works {.vcenter}

::::::: roomy
:::::: msg-list
::: msg-item
**1. Three assigned reviewers read and score**\
Assigned partly on self-declared expertise (high / medium / low / not enough)
:::

::: msg-item
**2. The committee discusses and agrees a consensus score**\
Reviewers present; all other members are "panelists"
:::

::: msg-item
**3. Every member then scores privately**\
Final scores must stay within ±0.5 of consensus
:::
::::::
:::::::

::: footnote
CIHR Project Grant Peer Review Manual, cihr-irsc.gc.ca/e/49564.html
:::

::: notes
(~1:00) Brief walkthrough, all public information from CIHR's own manual. The key
quantity for us is step 3 minus step 2: how far does each member's final score sit
from the consensus? The plus/minus 0.5 rule bounds it, which matters for modeling.
NIH has a near-identical structure -- "readers" vs. "non-readers" -- which Valen
Johnson analysed in PNAS in 2008 [@johnson2008a].
:::

## Research questions {.vcenter}

::::::: roomy
:::::: msg-list
::: msg-item
**Aim 1: Expertise and engagement**\
Do reviewers vs. panelists, and high vs. low expertise, differ in how they deviate from consensus?
:::

::: msg-item
**Aim 2: Whose scores move?**\
Do those patterns differ by applicant characteristics?
:::

::: msg-item
**Aim 3: What if?**\
Would alternative funding rules (e.g., weighting by engagement) change who is funded?
:::
::::::
:::::::

::: notes
(~0:45) Three aims. Aim 1 is descriptive/etiologic about the process; Aim 2 asks
about fairness across applicants; Aim 3 is exploratory policy simulation. Be brisk --
the interesting part is how we are doing it.
:::

## Approach: bring the code to the data {.vcenter}

::::::: roomy
:::::: msg-list
::: msg-item
**Restricted application-level data**\
CIHR Funding Analytics holds it; we do not see identities
:::

::: msg-item
**Our code runs *inside* CIHR**\
Analysts run it and return results -- no interactive debugging
:::

::: msg-item
**So we simulate first**\
Build, test, and pre-specify the whole pipeline on synthetic data
:::
::::::
:::::::

::: notes
(~1:00) This is the open-science hook. We cannot share the real data, so what we
*can* share is everything else: the simulated data-generating process, the
analysis code, and a modeling strategy document, all public before the real run.
Code has to work first time on data we will never see, so simulation is not a luxury
here -- it is the only way to debug. It also works as a pre-registration of the
analysis.
:::

## A two-part model for a "spike and slab" outcome {.smaller}

:::::: {.columns .valign-center}
::: {.column width="50%"}
Outcome: $d_{ijk}$ = final score − consensus score

Many members simply adopt the consensus ($d = 0$); the rest vary within ±0.5.

**Part 1:** did they deviate at all?

**Part 2:** by how much, and in which direction, if they did?
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
$$
E[d] = \underbrace{P(\text{deviate})}_{\text{Part 1: Bernoulli}} \times \underbrace{E[d \mid \text{deviate}]}_{\text{Part 2: ordinal}}
$$

Bayesian multilevel models (`brms`), with committee, application and member effects

Both parts allow **role** and **expertise** to shift the *location* and, in Part 2, the *spread*
:::
::::::

::: notes
(~0:45) Technical slide -- keep it short. The outcome has a big spike at zero plus a
bounded continuous-ish part, and CIHR scores are on a one-decimal grid, so we split
it: a Bernoulli model for whether anyone deviates, and an ordinal model for the
magnitude. The interesting design choice is that we deliberately let role affect both
the mean and the dispersion -- flexible enough to find either, both or neither.
:::

## What the simulated data look like {.smaller}

```{r}
#| label: sim-fig
#| fig-width: 14
#| fig-height: 5.6

p1 <- d |>
  group_by(job, exp) |>
  summarise(p = mean(deviated), .groups = "drop") |>
  ggplot(aes(exp, p, fill = job)) +
  geom_col(position = position_dodge(width = 0.75), width = 0.7) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = job_cols) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent_format(accuracy = 1)) +
  labs(x = "Self-rated expertise", y = NULL, fill = NULL,
    title = "Share who deviate from consensus") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 18) +
  theme(panel.grid.minor = element_blank(), legend.position = "top")

p2 <- d |>
  filter(deviated == 1) |>
  ggplot(aes(deviation, fill = job)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 0.1, boundary = 0, colour = "white",
    alpha = 0.85, position = "identity") +
  facet_wrap(~job, ncol = 1, scales = "free_y") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = job_cols) +
  labs(x = "Final − consensus score", y = NULL,
    title = "Direction and size, among deviators") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 18) +
  theme(panel.grid.minor = element_blank(), legend.position = "none")

p1 + p2 + plot_layout(widths = c(1.15, 1))
```

::: footnote
**Simulated** data only -- built from public CIHR process descriptions; no real applicant or reviewer data are shown.
:::

::: notes
(~0:45) Everything on this slide is simulated. Left: deviation is more likely for
panelists and for people with less expertise -- that is what we put in. Right: among
those who deviate, panelists swing wider and slightly more negatively, following the
NIH pattern in Johnson 2008. The point is not the result; it is that our models can
recover what we built in, which is what we need to know before touching real data.
:::

## Lesson 1: draw the causal diagram *before* choosing covariates {.smaller}

:::::: {.columns .valign-center}
::: {.column width="55%"}
```{r}
#| label: dag-fig
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 4.2

dag_aim1 <- dagitty("dag {
  Expertise -> Role
  Expertise -> Deviation
  Role -> Deviation
}")

coordinates(dag_aim1) <- list(
  x = c(Expertise = 1, Role = 0, Deviation = 2),
  y = c(Expertise = -1, Role = 0, Deviation = 0)
)

par(mar = c(0.5, 2.5, 0.5, 2.5))
drawdag(dag_aim1, cex = 1.5)
```
:::

::: {.column width="45%"}
CIHR assigns the reviewer role partly *based on expertise*.

So **role is a mediator, not a confounder, of expertise's effect** -- and "adjusting for everything" would answer a different question than the one we ask.

Focal exposure: **role**. Expertise is then a genuine confounder.
:::
::::::

::: notes
(~0:45) A lesson that came out of simulating, not analysing. Once we wrote down how
reviewers actually get assigned -- expertise drives who becomes a reviewer -- the causal
structure changed which model answers which question. Mediator vs. confounder; a "Table
2 fallacy" trap if we had just thrown everything into one regression. Better to find
that out on simulated data than after CIHR runs our code once.
:::

## Lesson 2: the estimand decides what the model can see {.vcenter}

::::::: roomy
:::::: msg-list
::: msg-item
**Combining the two parts is a real decision**\
Averaging *signed* deviation can cancel to ≈ 0 even when groups differ a lot
:::

::: msg-item
**Location and spread are different questions**\
Panelists may sit lower, swing wider, or both
:::

::: msg-item
**Simulation makes that visible early**\
We now simulate both, and plan to report which survive in real data
:::
::::::
:::::::

::: footnote
Simulation calibrated to public CIHR information (committee sizes, reviewer workload) and to @johnson2008a.
:::

::: notes
(~0:30) Second lesson. In our first cut the simulated groups differed only in *spread*,
so the combined average signed deviation came out at essentially zero for everyone --
technically correct, substantively useless. That pushed us to simulate both a location
and a spread difference and to pre-specify a flexible model. [CONFIRM: add one line on
real-data status/timeline here if there are results or a date to mention.]
:::

## Why dedicated metaresearch funding matters {.vcenter}

::::::: roomy
:::::: msg-list
::: msg-item
**Access**\
Partnership with the funder itself makes evaluating the funder's own process possible
:::

::: msg-item
**Time to do it properly**\
Simulation, pre-specification and open code are slow -- and rarely rewarded in project grants
:::

::: msg-item
**Open science with sensitive data**\
A reusable template for "open code, closed data" evaluation that other funders can adopt
:::
::::::
:::::::

::: notes
(~1:15) Land the significance point. Three things this funding bought us. One, a
seat at the table with CIHR's analytics team -- you cannot study a review process
from the outside with this granularity. Two, the time to do the unglamorous work:
simulation, a public modeling strategy, code that runs remotely. Three, a template:
the same approach could be reused by any funder that cannot release applicant-level
data. Emphasize that the RoR joint initiative (SSHRC, CIHR, Michael Smith Health
Research BC) is what made this a fundable thing to do rather than a side project.
:::
